parent.name: King's Indian Defense
parent.overview: Black fianchettoes the dark-squared bishop, castles and lets White build a big pawn centre (c4, d4, e4), then attacks it with ...e5 or ...c5 while preparing kingside play. In the main Classical/Mar del Plata structure the centre locks after d5 and the game becomes a race: White expands on the queenside with c4-c5 while Black storms the kingside with ...f5-f4 and ...g5. Other White systems change the picture: Samisch (f3) is aggressive with opposite-side castling attacks, Four Pawns (f4) maximises space, Averbakh (Bg5) keeps ...e5 in check, and the Fianchetto (g3) is quieter and positional. Sources describe it as dynamic, exceptionally complex and moderately risky for both sides, with a heavy theory burden because White has many fifth-move systems. Considered sound today after being held suspect until the 1930s.

parent.name: Slav Defense
parent.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 c6 3. Nc3 dxc4
parent.overview: Black supports d5 with ...c6 so that the centre is held by pawns while the light-squared bishop stays free to come out (usually to f5 or g4) before ...e6. The root is a crossroads: after 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 Black chooses the Pure Slav with ...dxc4 (active bishop, ...e5/...c5 breaks), the Semi-Slav with ...e6 (c6-d5-e6 triangle, theory-heavy and often sharp: Meran, Botvinnik, Anti-Meran), or the Chebanenko ...a6. White can also play the Exchange (cxd5 cxd5), a symmetrical structure with queenside minority attack ideas that has a drawish reputation, or quiet systems with 3.e3 or 3.Bf4. The Slav is played by many world champions (Botvinnik, Smyslov, Anand, Kramnik) and is regarded as sound; sources treat it as solid with room for counterplay rather than a forced-draw defence.

parent.name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit
parent.overview: White offers a pawn with 1.d4 d5 2.e4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3, aiming for rapid development, the open f-file and a kingside attack with Bc4, Nge2 or Bf4, castling, g4/h4 and Qe1-h4 ideas against h7. Black accepts with 4...exf3 5.Nxf3 and can choose among the Euwe (5...e6), Ziegler (5...c6), Teichmann (5...Bg4) and Bogoljubov (5...g6) defences, or decline with the Lemberger Countergambit 3...e5. With accurate defence Black consolidates the pawn, trades pieces and heads for a better endgame; engines and master opinion call White's compensation insufficient, which is why it is almost never seen at top level. Below master level it scores very well because the attack is easy to play and hard to defend against. The game is typically open and tactical.

parent.name: Four Knights Game
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Nc3 Nf6
parent.overview: Both sides develop both knights, so the root position is a symmetrical, classical tabiya from which White chooses the character of the game. The main branches are 4.Bb5 (the Spanish Four Knights), 4.d4 (the Scotch Four Knights), 4.g3 (the Glek System) and 4.Be2/4.Bc4 quieter alternatives. After 4.Bb5 Black can mirror with 4...Bb4 (the Double Spanish, highly symmetrical and drawish) or go for the Rubinstein 4...Nd4 for imbalance; 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4 Bb4 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.Bd3 d5 leads to an open, more active game in which White usually keeps the initiative. The opening has a drawish reputation and often gives quiet positional play, although sharp variations (Belgrade Gambit, Halloween Gambit) exist. It was almost forgotten after the 1930s and enjoyed a renaissance in the 1990s; Short, Adams and Shirov have played it, and it is popular at club level because it needs little theory.

parent.name: King's Indian Defense: Normal Variation
parent.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 g6 3. Nc3 Bg7 4. e4 d6
parent.overview: This root is the King's Indian reached by the move order 1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.c4 (the same position as 3.Nf3 in the 2.c4 move order). It is not a distinct opening: it is the ordinary King's Indian, where Black fianchettoes with ...Bg7, castles, and strikes at White's centre with ...e5, ...c5 or ...f5. White's choice of set-up decides the character: the classical 4.Nc3 and e4 leads to the locked-centre opposite-wing race (c4-c5 against ...f5-f4), while the Fianchetto Variation (g3, Bg2, O-O, Nc3) is quieter, positional, and has less forcing theory. The data subtree groups 4.e4 Normal Variation lines (the majority of games) under this root, so it mixes both. Black's success depends on timing and coordination rather than automatic aggression.

parent.name: French Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...e6 and ...d5, accepting a pawn chain and a space deficit in return for a sound position, and then hits White's pawn centre at its base with ...c5. The fight is over the dark squares d4 and e5. Black's problem piece is the light-squared bishop on c8, hemmed in by the e6 pawn; Black solves it by exchanging it or rerouting it (...b6 and ...Ba6, or ...Bd7 with ...Bb5/a4). White typically uses extra space for a kingside attack (f4-f5, and in the Advance the g4/h4 ideas) or expands on the queenside with a3-b4. Play is slower and manoeuvring, with a lot of pawn-break play. It has a reputation for solidity but a cramped early game for Black. The Winawer (3.Nc3 Bb4) is the sharpest branch, the Advance is the main fight in a locked centre, and the Tarrasch, Classical and Exchange are quieter. The root is one position after 1...e6 2.d4 d5; the structures differ strongly by branch.

parent.name: Nimzo-Larsen Attack
parent.overview: 1.b3 prepares Bb2 on the long diagonal, a hypermodern way to control the centre and pressure Black's kingside from the flank. Black's two main replies are 1...e5 (2.Bb2 Nc6 3.e3, the most common) and 1...d5 (2.Bb2 Nf6 3.e3, often a reversed Nimzo-Indian). White's usual set-up is e3, Nf3, Bb2 with flexible pawn play (f4, c4, d3, a kingside fianchetto), choosing a central plan after seeing Black's set-up. Black may take a big d5/e5 centre for White to undermine, contest d5 with ...c5/c4 English-style, or play London-like set-ups. Theory is light, most lines are rated roughly equal, and the play can turn tactical once the long diagonal and central files open. It is used as a surprise weapon by super-GMs, especially in online blitz.

parent.name: Scandinavian Defense
parent.overview: Black strikes at e4 at once with ...d5, and after 2.exd5 chooses between 2...Qxd5 (the 'positional' branch) and 2...Nf6 (the 'tactical' branch). In the main line 2...Qxd5 3.Nc3 the queen must move again, usually Qa5 (or Qd6, Qd8), and White gains time; Black answers with ...c6, ...Nf6, ...Bf5 or ...Bg4 and ...e6, reaching a solid, Caro-Kann-like c6/e6 structure with free piece play. White's lead in development and space is balanced by Black's sound, easily defended position, so the game is typically a quiet fight where White pushes for a slight edge. Sharp sidelines exist: the Portuguese (3...Bg4 after 2...Nf6 lines), Icelandic Gambit (2...Nf6 3.c4 e6) and the Marshall Gambit with 2...Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5 or 3...c6 ideas. It is objectively sound but has never been a mainstream elite weapon, though Carlsen, Anand and Larsen have used it.

parent.name: Alekhine Defense
parent.overview: Black attacks e4 at once with 1...Nf6 and, after 2.e5 Nd5, invites White to build a broad centre with c4, d4 and perhaps f4, planning to attack that centre later with ...d6, ...Nb6, ...Bg4, ...c5 and ...dxe5. White's job is to keep or use the extra space, either with the most ambitious Four Pawns Attack (4.c4 Nb6 5.f4), the popular Modern Variation 4.Nf3, or the less forcing Exchange 5.exd6; 2.Nc3 avoids the main line entirely. Positions lose symmetry from the start and are unbalanced, with a space edge for White against Black's counterplay on the overextended pawns. The opening is regarded as sound, original and tricky but risky (moderate to high), and is only moderately common at the top: Fischer, Korchnoi, Ivanchuk and occasionally Carlsen have played it.

parent.name: Old Indian Defense
parent.overview: The Old Indian (1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6, here reached by 1.d4 d6 2.c4) is the pre-fianchetto cousin of the King's Indian. Black sets up ...d6, ...e5, ...Nbd7, ...Be7, ...O-O and ...c6, aiming at a Philidor-like central structure that is solid and defensible but a little cramped. The main line is the Ukrainian Variation 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3 Nbd7 5.e4 Be7 6.Be2 O-O 7.O-O c6 8.Re1, where theory considers White slightly better. It has never been as popular as the King's Indian; the bishop on e7 is less active than a fianchetto. King's Indian players use it to sidestep the Samisch and Averbakh. The data root also holds the Neo-Old Indian / Modern set-up (1.d4 d6 2.c4 g6), which transposes to King's Indian or Pirc-like structures.

parent.name: Caro-Kann Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...c6 to support ...d5 and so challenges the e4 pawn with a sound pawn structure, while keeping the light-squared bishop free to come out to f5 or g4 before ...e6 (the French Defence's main drawback, at the cost of a tempo). Black accepts less space early and tends to get a resilient, hard-to-break structure with few weaknesses and good endgame prospects. Play is mostly positional and manoeuvring; it is called more solid and less dynamic than the Sicilian (s1). The Advance (3.e5 Bf5) and Panov-Botvinnik (3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4) lines are more combative, and the Advance became the most popular White try in the 21st century. Main branches: Classical (4...Bf5), Advance, Exchange, Panov, 4...Nf6 lines, Gurgenidze (...g6), Two Knights (2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3) and Fantasy (3.f3). This is a crossroads root after 1...c6; the pawn structures differ by branch.

parent.name: King's Gambit
parent.overview: 2.f4 offers a pawn at once to deflect Black's e-pawn, build a big centre with d4, develop quickly and use the half-open f-file against f7 (Bc4, Nf3, castling). The root covers both the Accepted lines (2...exf4: Kieseritzky 3.Nf3 g5 4.h4 g4 5.Ne5, Muzio, Bishop's Gambit 3.Bc4) and Declined lines (Falkbeer 2...d5, Classical 2...Bc5, and 2...d6 which is the most played move in the database). Accepted lines are sharp and tactically dense; Black tries to hold the pawn with ...g5 or return it with ...d5/...d6 to ease development. Declined lines are more solid and are chosen by stronger players who want to avoid the chaos. Play is open and double-edged for White's king as well.
